analogy.p: The skin, mucus and stomach acid are the walls, moat and gatehouse: they stop all intruders. Phagocytes are the guards inside who grab and remove any intruder. Lymphocytes are detectives that make a tailor-made key (antibody) for one intruder, and keep a photo (memory cell) so next time the response is instant. The analogy breaks down because real defences do not have intelligence; the shapes of molecules do the matching, and antibodies are made by cells in the body.

bullets: **Non-specific** = works the same way on every pathogen, e.g. skin, mucus, acid.
**Specific immune response** = targets one particular pathogen using its antigens (antibodies).
Four defence sites to know: **skin, nose, trachea and bronchi, stomach**.
Three white blood cell actions: **phagocytosis, antibody production, antitoxin production**.
Key idea: after the first infection, **memory lymphocytes** let the body respond faster and with more antibodies the next time.
Typical marks: 1 to 2 for naming a defence, 4 for describing white cell actions, 6 for linking to vaccination and memory.
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: AQA 4.3.1.3 (human defence systems) asks you to know that the body has **non-specific defence systems** that act against all pathogens, and that if pathogens get past these the **immune system** destroys them. You must describe the role of the skin, nose, trachea and bronchi and stomach, and explain three ways that white blood cells defend the body. You also need to link this to what happens on a second infection with the same pathogen, because that is the basis of vaccination.

bullets: **First line (non-specific)**: stops entry. Includes skin, mucus, cilia, stomach acid.
**Second line**: white blood cells destroy pathogens that have entered.
Pathogens enter through the **mouth, nose, cuts in the skin** and other openings; each has a defence.
A defence is **non-specific** if it does not need to recognise the pathogen first.
Pathogens make us ill by **reproducing rapidly** and by producing **toxins**, which damage cells and tissues.
Link: the more quickly the immune response occurs, the fewer symptoms you notice.
core.h: Two lines of defence: a big picture
core.p: Think of the body as a castle. The first line of defence is the walls and gates: structures and chemicals that stop microorganisms getting in at all. If a pathogen does get through, the second line of defence is the soldiers inside: the white blood cells of the immune system. The first line is the same for every invader; the second line is partly general (phagocytes) and partly tailor-made (antibodies from lymphocytes). Because pathogens reproduce rapidly in the body, the immune system must act quickly or the number of pathogens will overwhelm it.

bullets: Skin = **physical barrier** against pathogens.
**Platelets** help the blood clot to form a **scab**, sealing cuts.
A clot is made when platelets stick together with a protein mesh (fibrin) at the damaged area; you only need the idea that it seals the wound.
Burns and deep cuts are dangerous because the barrier is broken.
Link: blood components (plasma, platelets, red and white cells) are in the transport topic.
Exam phrase: 'skin acts as a barrier; platelets clot the blood to seal cuts'.
core.p: The skin covers the outside of the body and acts as a **physical barrier** that most microorganisms cannot pass through. It also has an outer layer of dead cells that are constantly shed, which removes pathogens that have settled there. If the skin is cut, **platelets** in the blood help the blood to **clot** quickly, forming a scab that seals the wound so pathogens cannot enter. This repairs the barrier and limits infection.

bullets: **Nose hairs** trap larger particles.
**Mucus** is sticky and traps smaller particles including **microorganisms**.
Trapped pathogens are removed by blowing or sneezing or swallowed (and killed by stomach acid).
This explains why breathing through the nose is better than through the mouth.
Do not say the nose 'kills' pathogens: it **traps** them.
Link to spread: coughs and sneezes also release droplets, so covering the mouth and nose reduces spread.
core.p: The nose is a main entry point because we breathe in air full of dust and microorganisms. The nose contains **hairs and mucus** that trap particles (dust, bacteria, viruses) in the air before they reach the lungs. The mucus is then swallowed or blown out, so the trapped microbes are removed. This is non-specific because it traps anything that enters.

bullets: **Mucus** traps pathogens in the airways.
**Cilia** move the mucus (with the trapped microbes) towards the throat.
The mucus is then **swallowed** and the stomach acid kills the pathogens.
**Smoking** damages and paralyses cilia, so mucus builds up and infections are more likely (smokers cough more).
Pathogens are trapped by mucus, not killed by the cilia.
Link: the gas exchange system in the lungs depends on a clean airway.
core.h: Trachea and bronchi: mucus and cilia
core.p: The trachea (windpipe) and bronchi (tubes into the lungs) are lined with cells that make **mucus** and with **cilia**, tiny hair-like structures. The mucus **traps pathogens** and dust from the air that was breathed in. The cilia beat in a coordinated way to move the mucus **upwards to the back of the throat**, where it is swallowed, so that the pathogens do not reach the lungs. This is called the mucociliary escalator.

bullets: Stomach acid = **hydrochloric acid** (never 'stomach enzymes kill pathogens').
It **kills** microorganisms in food and swallowed mucus.
Acid conditions are **non-specific**: they harm all pathogens that cannot tolerate them.
Some bacteria survive stomach acid, which is why food poisoning can still occur.
Link to enzymes: pepsin (a protease) works best at an acidic pH.
Exam phrase: 'hydrochloric acid in the stomach kills pathogens'.
core.p: The stomach produces **hydrochloric acid**, which makes the contents very acidic (about pH 2). Most pathogens that are swallowed in food, water, or mucus from the airways are **killed by the acid**. This protects the intestines from infection. Enzymes in the stomach (such as protease) work well at low pH, so the acid has two jobs: killing pathogens and helping digestion.

bullets: **Phagocytes** engulf and digest pathogens (phagocytosis).
**Lymphocytes** produce **antibodies** (and antitoxins) specific to a pathogen's antigens.
Each pathogen has unique **antigens**: molecules (proteins) on its surface that the immune system recognises as foreign.
White blood cells are fewer in number than red cells but increase during infection.
Higher-tier thinking: immune responses are specific because lymphocytes have receptors with shapes that match one antigen.
Link: HIV attacks white blood cells, which is why it weakens the immune system.
core.h: White blood cells: the immune system
core.p: If pathogens get past the first line, **white blood cells** attack them. White blood cells are made in bone marrow and carried in the blood and tissues. You must know three ways in which they protect us. Phagocytes act on any pathogen, while lymphocytes target a particular pathogen using antibodies, and also release antitoxins. This is the main difference between the non-specific and specific responses.

bullets: Step 1: phagocyte **detects** and moves towards the pathogen.
Step 2: the cell **engulfs** the pathogen, wrapping its membrane around it.
Step 3: the pathogen is enclosed in a **vacuole**.
Step 4: **enzymes** break down the pathogen, destroying it.
Phagocytosis is **non-specific**, while antibodies are **specific**.
Exam tip: use the words 'engulf' and 'digest', and do not say 'eat' or 'absorb'.
core.p: In phagocytosis a phagocyte **engulfs** the pathogen, taking it into the cell in a vacuole, and then **digests it** with enzymes. This is a non-specific response because the phagocyte does not need to know exactly which pathogen it is. It happens quickly at the site of infection and is also used to clear up pathogens that have been marked by antibodies.

bullets: **Antigen**: a molecule on the surface of a pathogen that triggers an immune response.
**Antibody**: a protein made by lymphocytes that binds to a specific antigen.
Antibodies are **specific**: an antibody for measles will not work on influenza.
Binding causes **clumping (agglutination)**, so phagocytes can destroy many pathogens at once.
Once the infection is cleared, antibody levels fall.
Lymphocytes can make antibodies fast the second time because of **memory cells**.
core.p: Every pathogen has **antigens** on its surface. When a pathogen enters, **lymphocytes** that match its antigens are stimulated to produce **antibodies**. Antibodies are proteins whose shape is **complementary** to one antigen, so each antibody is specific to a pathogen. They bind to the antigens, which can cause the pathogens to **clump together** and marks them for destruction by phagocytes. Antibodies are produced rapidly if the same pathogen enters again.

bullets: Toxin = a poison produced by a pathogen.
**Antitoxin** = a protein that neutralises a toxin.
Antitoxins do not kill the pathogen.
Tetanus and diphtheria are examples where toxins cause harm.
Exam point: 'antitoxins neutralise toxins'.
Link: some vaccines are against toxins.
core.p: Some bacteria cause illness through the **toxins** they release. White blood cells (lymphocytes) can produce **antitoxins** that bind to the toxins and **neutralise** them, preventing them from damaging cells. Antitoxins are therefore different from antibodies: antibodies attack the pathogen, antitoxins attack the poison it makes.

bullets: **Primary response**: slow and small, so symptoms appear.
**Secondary response**: **quick and large** because of memory lymphocytes.
Memory cells are specific to one antigen, so a measles infection does not protect against influenza.
Some pathogens (influenza) change their antigens, so new vaccines are needed.
Vaccination causes the primary response without disease.
Exam point: 'memory cells' or 'memory lymphocytes', not 'memory antibodies'.
core.h: Memory cells and the secondary response
core.p: After an infection, some lymphocytes remain as **memory cells**. If the same pathogen enters the body again, memory lymphocytes recognise its antigens and produce the correct antibodies **much faster and in larger amounts**. This is the **secondary response**, so the pathogen is destroyed before you develop symptoms. This is why you do not usually get the same infection twice, and it is the basis of vaccination.

bullets: Read **peak heights** and **times** from the axes carefully.
Compare: the second peak is higher and begins sooner.
**Ratio** = larger value ÷ smaller value (e.g. 200 ÷ 20 = 10 times higher).
Explain: memory lymphocytes produced antibodies faster.
The first response has a **lag phase** before antibodies increase.
Do not say the antibodies 'remember'.
core.p: A common data question shows antibody concentration against time for a first and second infection. The second peak occurs sooner after infection and is much higher, which shows the secondary response. To get full marks, you should use the data (peak height and time) and explain with memory cells. Remember to compare using numbers and units.

bullets: **Phagocyte**: engulfs and digests; non-specific; first on the scene.
**Lymphocyte**: makes antibodies and antitoxins; specific; produces memory cells.
**Antibody** vs **antitoxin**: one binds antigens on pathogens, the other neutralises toxins.
Both work together: antibodies tag pathogens for phagocytes.
Neither is a red cell: red cells carry oxygen.
Link to blood topic: white cells are found in the plasma and tissues.
core.p: It helps to build a comparison because exam questions often ask which cell does what. Phagocytes are quick and general, while lymphocytes are slower the first time but specific and can leave memory. Both are white blood cells and both are needed.

bullets: **Vaccination**: uses dead or inactive pathogen to cause antibody production and memory cells.
**Antibiotics**: help the immune system by killing bacteria; no effect on viruses.
**Monoclonal antibodies**: antibodies made in the lab to bind a specific antigen.
**Enzymes**: phagocytes use enzymes; stomach protease works in acid.
**HIV**: reduces lymphocytes so the immune response fails.
**Fever and inflammation**: part of the body's response, but not required at this level.
core.p: Defence systems connect with vaccination (artificial primary response), antibiotics (kill bacteria not viruses), monoclonal antibodies (specific antibodies for tests and treatment), and with disease spread. Good 6-mark answers make these links.

exam: **Command words**: 'Describe' = steps in order; 'Explain' = why using because/so; 'Compare' = similarity and difference.
**1 mark**: name a defence (skin, mucus, stomach acid) or white blood cell action.
**2 marks**: defence plus how it works, e.g. 'hydrochloric acid in the stomach (1) kills pathogens (1)'.
**3 marks**: three ways white blood cells protect: phagocytosis, antibodies, antitoxins, each with a few words of detail.
**4 marks**: describe phagocytosis or antibody action in steps with the key words engulf, digest, antigen, specific.
**6 marks**: link non-specific defences to the immune response, memory cells, and secondary response.
For graph questions: quote **both peaks with units**, calculate a ratio or time difference, then explain with memory lymphocytes.
Always include the words **'specific to the pathogen'** when describing antibodies.
Write 'engulf and digest' for phagocytosis; 'neutralise' for antitoxins; 'trap' for mucus.
Do not confuse **antigen** (on pathogen) with **antibody** (made by you).

mistakes.r: Antibodies bind to antigens (causing clumping and marking pathogens); phagocytes engulf and digest.
mistakes.w: Antibodies kill pathogens by eating them.

mistakes.r: Hydrochloric acid in the stomach kills pathogens.
Mucus traps pathogens and cilia move the mucus away from the lungs.
Antibodies are specific; only those matching the pathogen antigens are made.
mistakes.w: The body makes antibodies after any pathogen enters.

mistakes.r: Memory lymphocytes remain; they remember by making antibodies faster.
Antitoxins neutralise the toxins produced by bacteria.
Skin is a barrier; clotting seals cuts.
White cells defend; red blood cells carry oxygen.
Divide the larger value by the smaller to say how many times bigger.
mistakes.w: Ratio calculated smaller divided by bigger.

summary: Know the body's **non-specific defences** (skin, nose, trachea and bronchi, stomach) that stop pathogens entering, and how the **immune system** destroys any that get in using white blood cells: **phagocytosis, antibody production and antitoxin production**. This underpins vaccination, antibiotics and almost every infection question, and examiners expect precise vocabulary such as antigen, antibody and memory lymphocytes.

terms.d: A defence that acts against all pathogens in the same way.
A white blood cell that engulfs and digests pathogens.
The process in which a white blood cell engulfs a pathogen and digests it.
A white blood cell that produces antibodies and antitoxins.
A protein on the surface of a pathogen that causes the immune system to respond.
A protein produced by lymphocytes that binds to a specific antigen and helps destroy the pathogen.
A protein produced by lymphocytes that neutralises toxins.
A poison produced by a pathogen.
A lymphocyte that stays in the body after infection and allows a faster response next time.
Tiny hair-like structures that move mucus in the airways.
A sticky liquid that traps particles and microorganisms.
A cell fragment in the blood that helps blood clot.
The acid in the stomach that kills pathogens.
The body system, mostly white blood cells, that destroys pathogens that get into the body.

worked.ans: Phagocytes engulf pathogens and digest them (1). Lymphocytes produce antibodies that are specific to the antigens on the pathogen (1) and bind to it, helping destroy it (1). Lymphocytes also produce antitoxins that neutralise the toxins released by pathogens (1).
worked.q: Describe how white blood cells protect the body from pathogens. (4 marks)
steps: Antibodies: specific to antigens, cause clumping.

worked.ans: The second peak was 10 times higher (1) and 9 days sooner (1). This is because memory lymphocytes remained after the first infection (1), so the correct antibodies were produced more rapidly and in larger quantity (1).
worked.q: The first infection with a pathogen produced a peak of 20 arbitrary units of antibody after 14 days. A second infection produced a peak of 200 units after 5 days. How many times higher was the second peak, and explain why it was higher and quicker. (4 marks)
steps: Explain: memory lymphocytes made antibodies faster in larger amounts.

worked.ans: The lining of the trachea makes mucus that traps pathogens (1). Cilia beat to move the mucus to the back of the throat (1) where it is swallowed, so the pathogens do not reach the lungs and are killed by stomach acid (1).
worked.q: Explain how the trachea helps to protect the lungs from pathogens. (3 marks)
